question: With the EU strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life and the 2021–2027 Multiannual Financial Framework, the EU has increased its funding for combating antisemitism. It is important to take stock at this juncture and evaluate the state of play after three years. 1.
How much funding was requested for each project, broken down by Member State the project was located in, EU program and year (2021–2023)?
How much funding was granted for each project, broken down by Member State the project was located in, EU program and year (2021–2023)?

When making decisions about how to allocate the funding, does the Commission consider the regional differences in the number of anti-Semitic incidents or other factors for measuring the regional severity of antisemitism?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2024) The fight against antisemitism is funded under various funding programmes in direct or in indirect management mode, which makes it difficult to gather precise figures at Commission level.

As a follow-up to the adoption of the EU strategy on combatting antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (2021-2030)1 funding under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values increased from approximately EUR 5.2 million in 2021, to EUR 6 million in 2022, and EUR 11 million in 2023. 61 projects were funded over the three years for an average of EUR 360 000 per project.

Some projects combating antisemitism may also address racism and other forms of intolerance. The Member States where the beneficiaries of funding were located can be broken down as follows: Belgium and Poland with over EUR 3.5 million each, Germany with 2.5 million, Italy, France and Spain with about 1.6 million each. Between EUR 1-1.

5 million was given to projects carried out by beneficiaries in Sweden, Croatia and Greece. Beneficiaries from other EU countries received less than EUR 500 000. Grants under the programme are awarded following open calls for proposals that specify the criteria for evaluation. Submitted proposals are evaluated by independent experts against the published award criteria of relevance, quality and impact.
Based exclusively on this evaluation, proposals are ranked and funded up to the limit of available funding.
